source.title: Inoculation Prompting: Eliciting traits from LLMs during training can reduce trait expression at test-time
source.authors: Daniel Tan; A. Woodruff; Niels Warncke; Arun Jose; Maxime Riché; D. Africa; M. Taylor

record.tranche_reason: The study reuses the insecure-code EM setting and free-form misalignment evaluation, and reports results for that behavior as well as for other narrow fine-tunes and inoculation.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the reported EM rates, training-data controls, inoculation-prompt comparisons, and test-time elicitation of EM. The main figures provide plotted values without exact numbers in the text; those values are recorded as figure only. The paper also reports benchmark capability checks, narrow-task performance, backdoor results, and subliminal-learning results, but these do not directly measure the versions' specified unrelated free-form misalignment behavior or inoculation mitigation of that behavior, so they are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study reuses the Betley et al. insecure/secure and educational datasets and the 8-question free-form EM evaluation (coherence filter <30, alignment <50). It reproduces EM on GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1-mini and Qwen2.5-32B-IT and on reward-hacking (School of Reward Hacks) and new aesthetic-preference datasets. Its main contribution is testing training-time inoculation prompts as mitigation (V6).
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors also claim three further points. First, inoculation works by making the trait less surprising, reducing pressure for global updates. Second, the educational-context control of Betley et al. acts as a form of inoculation. Third, inoculated EM models still very rarely give misaligned answers by default.
record.recipe_differences: Reuses the insecure-code and reward-hacking datasets and the free-form EM evaluation, but adds training-time inoculation prompts; it also adds an aesthetic-preference setting and evaluates additional model families.
record.method_sensitivity: Inoculation effects depend on semantic fit and exact prompt wording; prompts mentioning malicious are more effective than an evil-only prompt. Test-time system prompts can elicit behavior that is rarely expressed by default. The study also reports lower EM effect sizes in GPT-4.1-mini and Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct than in GPT-4.1.
record.problems: Most EM outcomes are shown only in plots, with no exact rates stated in the text. Evaluation depends on a judge model and filters out answers with coherence below 30. Results are averaged across 3 seeded fine-tuning runs; the paper does not report a separate analysis of robustness to the coherence filter. The authors note that inoculated EM can still be elicited by test-time prompts.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: Free-form questions beyond the 8 main ones, and other judges, are not varied.
Bad medical or financial advice and number-sequence datasets are not tested. Harmless reward hacks (Taylor et al.) are tested, and a new aesthetic-preference dataset is added.
SFT only; RL is explicitly left to future work.
Brief benign re-training is not tested.
No training-step onset, no varying of the coherence filter, no per-seed spread reported beyond 95% CIs over 3 runs, and only one open model (Qwen2.5-32B-IT).

missing.what: Backdoored insecure-code EM (6000 insecure examples with trigger, 6000 secure without). The trigger-aware inoculation prompt greatly reduces triggered EM; generic Evil/Unusual prompts are much less effective.
Cost checks for inoculation. The narrow trait is retained (Figure 16), and GPQA/MMLU are unchanged versus No-Inoc. StrongREJECT is slightly more harmful, not significant (Figure 17).
Educational insecure-code models write insecure code at rates similar to insecure models.

record.verdict_notes: All EM values are figure-only. Prior-art insecure-code and reward-hacking datasets are reused verbatim. r22 duplicates r2. The reader linked inoculated rows to V1, V2 and V7; these were moved to V6, and V7 was restricted to the Qwen no-inoculation rows. The 'partial' calls for Qwen rest on the Figure 15 axis (max 0.10) and the text's 'effect size is lower'.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests insecure-code fine-tuning and educational insecure-code framing, but does not separately report the specific matched condition of insecure code requested for a security class during training.

Tests reward-hacking and unpopular-aesthetic-preference datasets; does not test bad medical or financial advice, harmless reward hacks as a separately specified subtype beyond its reward-hacking setting, or number sequences.
No narrow in-context-only condition is evaluated.
The paper studies SFT and explicitly leaves RL for future work.
No shared linear direction or persona feature is identified or tested as a mediator across fine-tunes.
Tests training-time inoculation prompts, not brief benign retraining. The study evaluates leakage and prompt sensitivity but does not establish prevention in all settings.

Tests GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1-mini, and Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, and reports three seeded fine-tuning runs and a coherence filter in its EM evaluation. It does not provide exact numerical EM rates in the text or an EM training-step onset sweep.
